title: Water on the move: how it joins places

files.lesson.md: --- order: 2 unit: water title: "Water on the move: how it joins places" node: AC9HG7K01 n2 summary: Trace water through a catchment, distinguish its forms, and explain what it carries between places. language: maths hook: A town has had no rain, but its river turns muddy. How could a change somewhere else reach it? --- Water can be **surface water** in rivers and lakes, **soil moisture** held in soil, or **groundwater** in spaces and cracks below ground. It can also be salt water, ice or invisible water vapour. A form tells us where or how water exists; a pathway tells us where it moves. **Runoff** flows over the ground. Water can also soak in and move underground, or evaporate, travel in the air and fall as rain elsewhere. A **catchment** is the area that drains towards a river or other outlet. **Upstream** is towards a river's source; **downstream** is towards its mouth. ## Predict: mud without rain ```step stage: predict insight: Notice that a place can receive consequences from somewhere else. check: type: predict q: In made-up Kerrin, the town has no rain but its river turns muddy. What could explain it? options: - Rain washed soil off a farm upstream - Only rain over the town can affect its river - River water cannot carry soil - All the mud must have formed in the town actual: Rain upstream can wash soil into the river. Flow can carry it to the town even when the town has no rain. ``` ## Try: follow the water ```step stage: run insight: Distinguish water stores before explaining connections. check: type: match q: Match each description in Kerrin to its water form. pairs: - - Water between soil particles around roots - Soil moisture - - Water in cracks in rock below the soil - Groundwater - - Water flowing past the town in the river - Surface water explain: The stores differ by where water is held. They can be connected by water movement. ``` Imagine rain soaking into the farm soil. Some stays around roots, some moves deeper into rock, and some runs into the river. These are made-up observations, not a report about a real place. ## Worked example: more than a direction ```step stage: investigate insight: Explain a connection as a pathway, something carried and another place affected. tasks: - check: type: question q: In Kerrin, rain washes loose soil off the farm. Why might the town downstream care? options: - The river can carry soil to the town’s water intake - Every place on the river must have identical rain - The town can only be affected by its own land - Soil cannot travel beyond the farm boundary answer: 0 feedback: - null - River connections do not mean identical weather. - Follow the flow from the farm to the town. - Flow can carry loose particles beyond a boundary. explain: The farm and town are connected by surface water carrying soil, with a consequence for water quality. smaller: check: type: question q: Muddy water flows along a gutter. What could reach a drain farther along? options: - Water with some of the mud - Only perfectly clean water answer: 0 feedback: - null - Flow can carry particles as well as water. explain: Moving water can carry material from one place to another. hint: - Find the farm and town on the picture. - Trace the river between them. - Name something that can travel with the water. - check: type: bug code: working.txt#nib text: Nib explains the case. Click the first line where the reasoning goes wrong. answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: water-is-only-transport explain: Line 3 ignores the loose soil moving water can carry. Explain what travels and why another place could care. ``` ### What reaches the town? ```worked \text{Start} :: Rain washes litter into a made-up school gutter. \text{Pathway} :: Water flows along the gutter towards a creek. \text{Transfer} :: Flow carries litter from the school to the creek. \text{Connection} :: A change at school can affect water quality in the creek. ``` ### Find Nib’s slip ## Vary: forms and pathways ```step stage: modify insight: Apply the connection idea to a real river and different forms. tasks: - check: type: question q: On the real-river card, which pathway joins the named places? options: - Murrumbidgee headwaters to its junction with the Murray - Murray junction to Murrumbidgee headwaters - The rivers have no surface-water connection - Every river journey must first pass through the air answer: 0 feedback: - null - Follow the direction from headwaters towards the junction. - A junction is where river channels join. - Evaporation is one pathway, not a step in every river journey. explain: The Murrumbidgee carries surface water from its headwaters towards the Murray. - check: type: match q: Match the other forms to a possible pathway. pairs: - - Ice on a slope - Melts, then runs into a stream - - Salt water at the sea surface - Evaporates; water vapour travels in air - - Water vapour in the air - Cools and condenses; water may fall as rain elsewhere explain: Water can become a resource elsewhere after moving or changing form. Evaporation leaves most dissolved salts behind. ``` ### A real river connection Parks ACT describes the **Murrumbidgee River** flowing from headwaters in Kosciuszko National Park to its junction with the **Murray River** near Balranald. This is the real pathway. The muddy farm and town in Kerrin are made up; they are not claims about the Murrumbidgee. *Source: [Murrumbidgee River Corridor (Parks ACT)](https://www.parks.act.gov.au/find-a-nature-park/murrumbidgee-river-corridor), checked 30 October 2026.* ### Other forms can move too ## Practise: explain what travels ```step stage: practise insight: Explain a pathway and what is transferred. tasks: - check: type: question q: In a made-up case, a spill soaks into rock beside a village. Groundwater moves towards a spring at another village. Why might the second village care? options: - Dissolved pollution could travel to its spring - Groundwater stays still because it is underground - Underground water is always safe to drink - Only a shared road can connect the villages answer: 0 feedback: - null - Groundwater can move through connected pores and cracks. - Being underground does not guarantee clean water. - The pathway here is groundwater, not a road. explain: A connection can be underground. Name the pathway and what it carries. - check: type: question q: Which explanation goes beyond saying water flows downhill? options: - Runoff carries fertiliser from a field to a lake, affecting water quality - The river flows from high land to low land through the catchment - There is water in the river and a lake farther downstream - The river and the lake are both stores of surface water answer: 0 feedback: - null - This gives direction but no transferred material or consequence. - This names places without explaining what is transferred. - This classifies stores without explaining a connection. explain: Name the starting place, pathway, material and receiving place. ``` ### An underground connection ### More than downhill ## Make: explain one connection ```step stage: make insight: Produce a specific connection, not a list of terms. check: type: reflect text: In my own book I named three water forms, traced one pathway between two named places in Kerrin, and explained what the water carries and why the receiving place could care. A partner or teacher read it. ``` Use the made-up Kerrin picture. Draw arrows and write two or three sentences. Include the water form, starting place, receiving place and something carried or affected. Write in your book, not on this page. ## Typical: through soil, rock and air ```step stage: make insight: Widen pathways while keeping the connection reasoning. check: type: reflect text: In my book I explained two made-up connections, one through soil or rock and one through the air, including how salt water, ice or vapour could become a usable resource elsewhere. tier: typical ``` Imagine groundwater feeding a spring after rain soaks into a hillside. In another case, sea water evaporates and vapour travels inland before rain falls. Explain the forms and pathways. ## Wider: one connection at two scales ```step stage: make insight: Transfer the same reasoning between scales. check: type: reflect text: I explained how litter could travel from a school gutter to a creek and how dissolved pollution could travel through a larger made-up river system. I named a receiving place in each. tier: wider ``` Both cases are made up. Keep the explanation pattern even though the distances differ. Typical and wider steps are extras on the same idea. You do not need them to finish the lesson. ```teacher summary: Trace water through a catchment, distinguish its forms, and explain what it carries between places. time: 40 timing: Predict and Try 8 min · Worked example 12 min · Vary 8 min · Practise 6 min · Make 6 min. Optional width is extra. goals: - I can distinguish surface water, soil moisture and groundwater. - I can trace one pathway between two places. - I can explain what water carries and why another place is affected. struggle: Students may stop at “water flows downhill”. Ask what travels with it and who or what receives it. Give time to add the missing link. before: Usually Year 7. This is the second hinge. K02 and K03 depend on seeing water as a connection rather than a static store. The untiered path distinguishes three forms and explains one surface pathway. Protect the farm-to-town question before moving on; the gutter lead-in strips back the same idea. Kerrin, its schematic, spill and other scenarios are made up. Only the Parks ACT card describes real places. It establishes a route, not the fate of every drop or a claim about pollution. No Australian water-distribution or climate-system study is needed. running: - "Try: trace the flow arrows and distinguish soil moisture from groundwater." - "Worked example: ask for start, pathway, carried material and receiving place." - "Vary: separate the real river route from the invented farm case." - "Make: read the book explanation before accepting the tick." stuck: - see: The answer only says water flows downhill. ask: What could move with it, and where might it arrive? fix: Add a carried material and a consequence for a receiving place. - see: Soil moisture and groundwater are treated as identical. ask: Is it around roots in soil or in spaces in deeper rock? fix: Name the store before tracing movement. - see: Underground water is assumed clean. ask: Could dissolved pollution enter where rain soaks in? fix: Groundwater can carry dissolved substances. support: "Use the smaller gutter question. Offer the oral frame: From __, water moves by __, carrying __ to __." stretch: Explain the same connection at gutter and river-system scales, without introducing a new concept. exit: q: Why might a town care about loose soil on an upstream farm? a: Rain can wash soil into the river. Surface water can carry it to the town, affecting water quality. explain: Water connects places when movement transfers materials or consequences. Name the start, pathway, something carried and receiving place. Surface water, soil moisture and groundwater describe different stores. sources: - title: Murrumbidgee River Corridor (Parks ACT) url: https://www.parks.act.gov.au/find-a-nature-park/murrumbidgee-river-corridor checked: 2026-10-30 leads: "Next: environmental, economic and social effects of water connections. Australian water distribution belongs to K02." class: inquiry: q: Can a town protect its river by caring for only the land inside its boundary? prompts: - What is your reason? - What information would change your view? notes: "Protect the hinge: direction alone is not enough. Ask for carried material and a receiving place." activities: - at: investigate kind: discussion title: Trace the missing link minutes: 5 do: Pairs trace from Kerrin’s farm to the town. The listener asks what travels with the water and why the town could care. Compare with a gutter-to-creek connection at school. notes: "Protect the hinge: direction alone is not enough. Ask for carried material and a receiving place." - at: make kind: activity title: Compare your explanations minutes: 4 do: Write in your own book, then swap with a partner. The partner identifies the geographical terms and one link explained with because. notes: The reflect tick records completion. The teacher or partner reads the writing; the site does not assess it. ```
